messages.subject: dealing with responsive movement
messages.body_plain:
Dear All,

I have a question relating to responsive movement during surveys. =
Movement violates the assumptions of the standard approach, and I would =
like to know if the following is a legitimate way around it. Please also =
correct any errors in my argument along the way.

The abundance estimate N=3Dn/P (where n is number of animals counted) =
depends on finding P, the unconditional probability of detection.

In distance sampling P is given by $g(x)h(x)dx, where $ means =
integration, g(x) is the detection function and h(x) is the probability =
density function of perpendicular distances to animals.=20

The standard assumption is that h(x) is uniform, so we get P=3D$g(x).dx =
/ w.

When there is responsive movement h(x) is no longer uniform and things =
go awry. Then g(x) and h(x) can't be estimated seperately because their =
effects are combined in the process which leads to the observed =
distances.

The idea I want to put to you relates to surveys in which there is =
responsive movement:  If independent experiments can be carried out in =
which there is no responsive movement so that g(x) can be estimated, =
then h(x) could be estimated on the standard survey using the 'prior' =
estimate of g(x). If g(x) and h(x) are known, abundance estimation is =
possible, despite the responsive movement.

To give a concrete example, in my case we are carrying out acoustic =
surveys for harbour porpoise and we are fairly sure that under normal =
conditions the noise of the boat's engine and the depth sounder alerts =
the porpoises and causes responsive movement. The independent experiment =
I have in mind then, in order to estimate g(x) seperately, is to carry =
out further surveys silently, by sailing (engine off) and with the depth =
sounder off.

Thankyou,

Justin (Matthews)

messages.subject: Re: dealing with responsive movement
messages.body_plain:
Hi Justin, list,

Yes, your approach should work, assuming the detection function is the same in
both survey modes (engine on and engine off).  Also, unless you expect density of
animals to be the same in both modes (e.g., from randomizing when you do the
experiment) I think you will need to assume that animals are not being attracted
from outside the surveyed strip.

David Borchers knows more about this than me, as he uses double-observer methods
where one observer is looking far ahead to estimate g(x) and h(x) simultaneously.
He's on holiday this week, but will probably fill in more details when he gets
back.

Cheers,

 - Len

messages.subject: Fwd: Re: Fwd: [DIST-SAMP] dealing with responsive movement
messages.body_plain:
Here was David's response to Justin's message:

==================BEGIN FORWARDED MESSAGE==================
> >From: "David Borchers" <d...@mcs.st-and.ac.uk>
> >Date: Thu, 10 Apr 2003 16:32:17 +0100

> >Then g(x) and h(x) can't be estimated seperately because their effects are
> >combined in the process which leads to the observed distances.

If you use double-platform methods (2 or more observers searching
independently of each other, with identification of those seen by both done by
some means), then you need not assume h(x) - you can estimate both g(x) and
h(x) from these data. Intuitive explanation: The proportion of animals at x
that are seen by both observers allows you to estimate g(x) without any
assumptions about h(x); given the estimate of g(x), you can reconstruct what
h(x) must have been to generate the distribution of distances you observed.

> >The idea I want to put to you relates to surveys in which there is responsive
> >movement:  If independent experiments can be carried out in which there is no
> >responsive movement so that g(x) can be estimated, then h(x) could be estimated
> >on the standard survey using the 'prior' estimate of g(x). If g(x) and h(x) are
> >known, abundance estimation is possible, despite the responsive movement.

> >To give a concrete example, in my case we are carrying out acoustic surveys for
> >harbour porpoise and we are fairly sure that under normal conditions the noise
> >of the boat's engine and the depth sounder alerts the porpoises and causes
> >responsive movement. The independent experiment I have in mind then, in order
to
> >estimate g(x) seperately, is to carry out further surveys silently, by sailing
> >(engine off) and with the depth sounder off.

The method relies crucially on the assumption that g(x) is the same in the two
cases. The validity of the assumption needs to be assessed in the context of
the application.

In your concrete example, I think the assumption that g(x) is the same when
the engine and depth sounder are on and when they are off may not be valid.
Because the boat will be stationary or near-stationary when the engine is off,
the detection funciton might be quite different in the two cases - for a
number of reasons. One reason is that for a species like harbour porpoise,
which is not continuously available for detection, the slower you go, the more
often any one animal will be available while in detection range. This will
make g(0) larger when the engine is off than when it is on and may also change
the shape of g(x).

If detections were visual, observers might behave differently when the boat is
stationary to when it is moving.

Animal movement also becomes more of an issue when the boat is stationary - on
average, animals will move over a wider span of perpendicular distances while
in detection range if the boat is stationary. The trajectories of the animals
relative to the observer depend on boat speed: all trajectories will be
parallel to transect line if the boat goes fast enough relative to the speed
of animal movement, compared to random directions (if the animals move in
random directions) when the boat is stationary. This could change the
detection function.

Hope this helps.

messages.subject: Lobster abundance survey
messages.body_plain:
Dear list members,

=20

I am struggling to find out a method to estimate (relative) lobster
abundance over a 12 year period. The survey does not use line transects,
but something very close to point transects. For the first year, about
500 sites were stratified randomly sampled. A diver swims 500 meters and
counts the number of lobsters within 4 meters wide. Certainly, no
lobster was found at many sites. In the following ten years, only 100
sites, which have the highest number of lobsters and constitute about
85% of the total number of the lobsters caught in the first year, were
repeated sampled each year, and the locations of the 100 sites were
fixed and relocated exactly by portable GPS. But, last year another
benchmark survey of 350 stratified randomly selected sties was carried
to detect possible changes in distribution. The purpose of the survey
was to establish a time series of relative abundance indices for the
population.

=20

My question is: can Distance be used for analyzing this kind of data? I
am only recently involved in analyzing the data. Any suggestion relevant
will be highly appreciated. Thank you very much in advance.

=20

Best regards

=20

YImin

=20

=20

=20

experience of distance sampling alongside researchers in the field, and =
potentially back in the lab around this time in Canada. =20

I was hoping you could give me some pointers on likely people/projects =
that will be up and running around March/April/May 2004.  I would aiming =

I currently work for Landcare Research based in New Zealand, as a research =
technician with interests in birds and mammals.  Guy Forrester, our =
